reaction: A storehouse before a storm, eight residents with limits. I like that people choose what they can manage. I want to know who they are before I start lifting boards.

Nora, 28, designs repairs; an older brother she is no longer close to. Then the panel reads like an instruction sheet: offer a break, wait five seconds, choose Invite conversation. Odd to be told the steps for kindness, but I will follow her first.

I did what it said: break, five seconds, invite. It just repeated the instruction back: spend a minute together first. I do not know what spending a minute together is as a button. Confused, and meanwhile seven people are standing idle.

A tidy little workshop map with eight figures. People come as one-line CVs: an accountant, an innkeeper who watches the river, an 18-year-old who tests games. I have put six to work and left Nora resting because I want to talk to her, but the steps to talk read like a recipe and my first try only bounced back the recipe. The clock runs about a game minute a second, so it is quick.

Help paused the game, which is kind. I think a minute together means a minute of play has to pass first, so I was simply too early. Mouse controls too: drag a box and right-click. I will try Nora again now.

Nora opened up: she left a feature out of a handle because she preferred the simpler shape, and never asked the person who would use it. That is a real, small confession; it lands. Now Offer a small collaboration lit up. I want to see if I can help her make that right.

Lovely. She marks the drawing unfinished and adds the grip back so a resident can try it. And it does not pretend: the handle still needs testing, and she and her brother are still distant. That is room to repair a mistake without a tidy bow. I want to find who might test the handle.

Dilek records kitchen sounds, a loose lid with a wonderful rattle, and leaves voices out unless people agree. The collaboration is just her making a recording for herself. Sweet and careful about consent. But I notice the pattern now: break, wait, invite, collaborate, one paragraph each. It feels like a little ritual I perform on each person.

Sam copied another player’s bug description into a report and said he had checked it when he had not. That one pricks a bit, given what I am doing right now. I notice every confession is a small professional failing, and each one is very tidy.
Nerys and her telescope; she will not promise clear skies. I like that she keeps her promises careful. Storehouse is now lit up, 190 boards and 121 bags. I will build.

The storehouse is started already at 2:36 with the storm at 10:00, so the pressure is gone, and the people are what I am here for. Four little confessions so far, each with a small repair that does not overclaim. I am enjoying it, though the ritual is getting mechanical.
Sevim is 69, a retired teacher, and I have had her hauling ballast bags and she is tired. I feel a bit bad. Break first.

Sevim. Widowed, her child abroad, and she called a pupil lazy before learning he was caring for a sick parent; she still has his exercise books and has never admitted it. That one actually got me. I want to give her more than a single button, but the button is what there is.

She drafts a private note admitting it and does not claim forgiveness. Good, respectful. But the first sentence, asking what makes this equipment card hard to use, came from nowhere. What equipment card? It reads stitched on.

Oskar staged a caption about a volunteer staying through a storm, while we are literally waiting for a storm. Same shape again: confession, small honest act, still needs to correct the old one. Six people, six versions of the same moral. I am starting to feel lectured gently, as though the residents are all one person in different coats.

Oh, that is nice: Dai leaves room for Nora to question his inspection card. The first time two of them touch each other. Maybe that is where Sevim’s equipment card came from too. I like the threads crossing; I wish they did it on screen rather than in a sentence.

Burak and his paper ferry, something that does not have to be useful. The one person without a confession; a relief, honestly. All eight heard now. What is left is the cabin and the storm. I am not sure what else there is for me to do with them.

Oops. Nora has been standing there waiting since 1:18, and I never noticed because nothing told me she was idle. I sent her and Dilek for boards for the guest cabin. The help said I can tap the workshop hub to invite a local helper; I want to try that.

Aylin arrives for 35 meals. No personal history is recorded for this helper. So the paid help is just a pair of hands. After eight people with inner lives, that line felt a bit cold. I will still say hello later.

Layout check at 360x690: the map shrinks to a thin strip with Workshop hub and Storehouse labels overlapping, and the name row is cut off at the right edge (Sevim half shown). My position tap on Nerys worked and added her to the selection with Aylin. Returning to 1280x800.

Storehouse is finished at 5:27, with nearly five game hours to spare. One status line, no little moment. I expected the residents to react, or someone to say something. Now what? I have ~4.5 real minutes until the storm, and nothing that feels urgent.
Main job done with hours to spare; the storm now feels like a formality. The residents were the good part and I have heard each of them once. Curious whether the storm itself shows anything.
Aylin has no history, and the invite just repeats spend a minute together. A helper with nothing to say, by design. That makes her feel like a trolley, not a person.

Oh, Nora is resting and will go back to boards on her own. So she was not idle and forgotten after all, or she found her own way back. I worried for nothing. The game is now mostly me watching people carry things.

input: About this resident, Invite conversation (Nora, second time)
reaction: Her record keeps what we did: the grip is back, the handle still needs testing, she and her brother are still distant. I like that it does not pretend everything is fixed. But inviting her again just gives me her food line. I think each person only has the one talk.

I have heard everyone once, the storehouse is built, and now I just send tired people to eat and they come back tired. I would close the laptop here. I will stay to see the storm, and to see whether the empty cabin brings anyone with a story.
Only another helper for 35 meals, and the last helper had no history. I would rather keep the meals for the nine I have. The empty cabin space will stay empty.
The storm will arrive in two minutes. Finish the storehouse. But the storehouse IS finished, it says so one line up. Now I second guess: is it really finished? A small jolt of worry I did not need.
Watching numbers climb towards a storm I am already ready for. The people have gone quiet.

The storm came and I never saw it. A card: supplies stayed dry. And the last words from the people I listened to are Nora and Sam saying I am tired, I need a break. After their confessions, that is what they get to say at the end? It lands flat.

9 people, 3 completed buildings. That is all. Nothing about the handle Nora fixed, the recording Dilek made, the telescope of Nerys. The talks did not count for anything on the last page. I still have time set aside, so I went back to the title to see whether a second go is different. (Logged late: first attempt failed on an apostrophe.)
Eight fresh local residents and conversations that take time. That is exactly what I wanted more of. Thirty minutes is more than I have left tonight, but I will start it and meet a few people.

It promised eight fresh local residents, and here are Nora, Sam, Dai, Nerys, Dilek, Burak, Sevim and Oskar again. Same names. Are they the same people who remember the handle and the telescope, or strangers wearing the names? I cannot tell yet.

A wall of new things: three places, view versus travel, private story, two people talking, yield the trolley route, a practice bout, heard accounts that may be withheld. And sentences I cannot parse: the framework fictional timetable, the current finite departure route supports the ten-minute chapter. Who is that written for? Not me. But Invite a private story and Invite two people to talk are what I came for. I will start with Nora.
I asked all eight and it says You asked Oskar. Only Oskar? Or is that just the last name? This is a request, not a completed outcome. I appreciate the honesty but I do not know who is actually going.

Sam and Nora disagree over the narrow trolley route. Now this is something I care about: two people at odds. I would rather they talk than order one to yield. It pays, Nora says of the ballast, which is a blunt little line.

I invited Sam and Nora to talk and the game said they were invited. Twenty minutes of their day later, nothing: no words between them, nobody yielded, only I am doing this out of habit. I am reading a log of my own requests.

input: Sam, Offer to yield the trolley route
reaction: You asked Sam to consider the selected activity. The selected activity? I asked a teenager to give way to an older woman, and it reads like a form. I will wait and see if he does.

Sam yields the route after choosing to make room. Good, a small kindness. And on the very next line: Dai and Nora disagree over the narrow trolley route. The same quarrel with a new name in it. Nora inspects the yard cache, three times now. Ballast bags still 7 after an hour and a half of their day. It feels like a rota of the same sentences, and nobody has said a word to anybody. I would close the laptop.

Return these carried materials to the workshop hub first. I asked her for a story and was told about her load. I do not know which materials, or where the hub is in this new map. Nora meanwhile says It pays. Confused, and a bit tired of being refused by paperwork.

Nora chooses to tell you: I left a feature out of a handle design... I did not ask the person who would use it. It is the same confession I heard in the first chapter. So she is not fresh, she is the same Nora telling it to me again as if we never fixed the grip together. Or she is a stranger with the same past. Either way it takes the shine off the first time.

reaction: Stopping here. The first chapter gave me eight people with a real confession each, and Nora and I fixing the grip was lovely. Then the storm came off stage, the last page counted only buildings, and the longer day handed me the same names, the same quarrel moving from Sam to Dai, and Nora telling me her handle story again as if it were new. I would not leave it running. I might come back another evening only if the people remembered what we did together.
